title: System Binary Proxy Execution: Msiexec
summary: Msiexec.exe is the command-line host for the Windows Installer service, signed by Microsoft and present on every Windows installation, and it executes installation packages with the .msi extension from local or network locations. Beyond ordinary package installation, it can apply transforms and patches, and it can be pointed at a library file to run a specific exported function, which gives an adversary several ways to reach code execution through a trusted binary. The most common abuse paths are installing an attacker-supplied package, including one retrieved from a remote share or a web address, and running a DLL through the installer interface, with quiet switches suppressing user interaction. A further escalation concern is the AlwaysInstallElevated policy: when enabled for both the machine and the user, any user can cause the installer to run with SYSTEM privileges, converting a user-level action into a privileged one. Detection depends on command line context, because msiexec runs routinely: quiet install switches combined with a file path or URL outside managed deployment shares, packages written to temporary or user-writable directories shortly before execution, msiexec as the parent of a command shell or script host, and network connections to hosts that are not part of normal software distribution. Legitimate deployment is usually driven by management tooling, uses signed packages from controlled locations, and matches a change record.

beginner.definition: msiexec.exe is the program Windows uses to install software packages that end with .msi. Microsoft signs the program, and it exists on every Windows computer. It can read a package from a folder, a network share, or a web address.
beginner.whyItMatters: A signed installer can install an attacker's package just as easily as a legitimate one. Packages can contain scripts that run during installation, so code executes without any extra tool. A Windows setting called AlwaysInstallElevated lets installations run with system rights, which is far more powerful than a normal user. If you ignore this, a routine-looking install can quietly take over a machine.
howItWorks: msiexec.exe is the program Windows uses to install software packages that end with .msi.
It can read a package from a local folder, a shared network folder, or even a web address.
Packages can contain scripts that run before, during and after the installation steps.
The program can also be pointed at a library file and asked to run a named function inside it.
If a Windows policy called AlwaysInstallElevated is switched on, the installation runs with system rights.
Attackers combine these features to install their own code using a program that looks completely normal.
beginner.example: A delivery driver holds a permanent pass for your building, because they bring parcels every week. Today the parcel is not on the order list, and inside is equipment that nobody ordered. The front desk waves the driver through, because the pass is genuine and familiar. AlwaysInstallElevated is like that driver also holding a master key, so the delivery can reach every floor of the building.
takeaways: A signed installer program can install an attacker's package just as easily as a legitimate one.
Quiet install switches and packages from user folders deserve a second look.
Check whether AlwaysInstallElevated is enabled, because it removes an important permission barrier.

objectives: Explain what msiexec.exe does and which input types it accepts.
Describe how an MSI package can carry code that runs during installation.
Explain how this sub-technique differs from the System Binary Proxy Execution parent technique.
Explain the risk created by the AlwaysInstallElevated policy setting.
Identify the command line and package path evidence that separates malicious installs from managed deployment.
